one_liner: Async C++17/20 HTTP/1.1 web framework on an epoll reactor; ~1.8-2x Go net/http req/s on hello-world.
what_it_does: A full-stack asynchronous HTTP/1.0/1.1 application framework (server and client) for C++17/20: routing to controllers declared with macros (HttpSimpleController, HttpController with {param} paths) or registerHandler lambdas, filters/middleware, sessions, WebSocket, CSP server-side views, async PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite/Redis clients with an ORM, and the drogon_ctl code generator. Handlers are callback-style (you call a std::function with an HttpResponsePtr) or C++20 coroutines, and the app is configured in code or from a JSON/YAML file. It is a different language and API from Go net/http, so adopting it means a rewrite, not a swap.
how_it_is_fast: It runs on trantor, a muduo-style one-event-loop-per-thread reactor: each IO thread owns an epoll (kqueue on macOS/BSD) loop, and on Linux each thread gets its own SO_REUSEPORT listening socket, so the kernel spreads accepts with no shared acceptor; cross-thread work is handed over through a lock-free task queue. Requests are parsed by a hand-written incremental HTTP/1.x state machine (CRLF scanning over a MsgBuffer) that drains every pipelined request from one read, and HttpRequestImpl objects are recycled per connection through a shared_ptr custom deleter. Exact-path routes are a hash-map lookup, and responses marked setExpiredTime(0) are rendered once and reused, with only the Date bytes patched once per second.
when_to_use: High-request-rate HTTP/1.1 REST/JSON APIs written in C++ where per-request framework overhead matters: 126K-135K req/s for an empty GET on 4 pinned cores, about 1.8-2x Go net/http in the same run.
Many concurrent keep-alive or pipelined clients on Linux, where every IO thread has its own SO_REUSEPORT listener and epoll loop.
Services that want async PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite/Redis access, an ORM, sessions and WebSocket in one framework; FastDbClient runs DB IO on the HTTP threads to avoid thread hops.
C++20 codebases that want coroutine handlers (co_await on DB and HTTP-client calls) instead of nested callbacks.
Cross-platform builds (Linux, macOS, BSD, Windows, ARM); CI covers GCC 9-13, Clang 11-17, MSVC on Windows 2022 and macOS 14/15.
when_not_to_use: You need an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 server: master speaks HTTP/1.0/1.1 only, and HTTP/2 exists only as a beta client (v1.10.0-beta.3).

Tail latency at modest concurrency matters more than peak req/s: in the same run Drogon's p99 at 64 connections was 9.8 ms, against 3.05 ms for net/http and 1.13 ms for Oat++, even though its median was 0.12 ms.

Handlers must call blocking libraries (sync DB drivers, sync HTTP clients, long CPU work): each loop is single-threaded, so you have to offload that work or rewrite it with async callbacks or coroutines.

Static-file serving or generated ORM RESTful controllers exposed to untrusted input without review: as of 2026-09-26 there are open reports of a %00 path-truncation bypass of the static-file extension allowlist (#2591; fix PR #2600 not merged) and of SQL injection via Mapper::orderBy() and the Criteria JSON constructor (#2575, #2576).
HTTP framing is not your bottleneck: the 2x is for an empty-body hello-world, the older-method master-branch run showed only about 1.2x, and header access copies into std::string maps (issue #2535).

integration.form: static lib (default; BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON builds a shared lib)
integration.dependencies: trantor (git submodule), jsoncpp >= 1.7, zlib, libuuid (or Boost.UUID). Optional: OpenSSL or Botan (HTTPS via trantor), Brotli, yaml-cpp, c-ares, libpq, MySQL/MariaDB client, SQLite3, hiredis
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 with a complete std::filesystem (CMake aborts otherwise); C++20 is auto-selected when <coroutine> exists and enables coroutines. CMake 3.5+. CI: GCC 9-13, Clang 11-17, MSVC (Windows 2022). The install doc still says gcc >= 5.4 and recommends 11+.
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll), macOS/FreeBSD/OpenBSD (kqueue), HaikuOS and Windows per the README; x86-64 and ARM. The per-thread SO_REUSEPORT listeners are Linux-only; other OSes use one accept thread that hands connections to the IO loops.
integration.thread_safety: Each connection belongs to one IO-loop thread, and its handlers run there. Work submitted from other threads (queueInLoop/runInLoop) goes through a lock-free queue, and a response produced on another thread (for example in a DB callback) is queued back to the connection's loop. Blocking a loop stalls every connection on it, and sync calls into a client on the same loop deadlock (threading FAQ).

gotchas: The benchmarked GET / never reaches the router: a registerSyncAdvice hook returns it before routing, filters and middleware run, and the config disables the Date and Server headers. A normal HttpController route does more work per request.
setThreadNum defaults to 1 IO thread, and 0 means std::thread::hardware_concurrency(). Set it explicitly, especially in CPU-limited containers (the benchmark used 0).

Paths are lowercased and matched case-insensitively. When the exact-path hash lookup misses, routes with {param} placeholders are found by a linear scan with std::regex_match over all regex routes, so cost grows with the number of parameterized routes.

Never block in a handler or DB callback: sleep or sync IO stalls every connection on that loop, and sync queries on a FastDbClient, which shares the HTTP IO threads, deadlock (threading FAQ, issue #1068).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Drogon over Oat++ when you want built-in async DB/Redis clients, an ORM and more hello-world throughput (1.09-1.34x Oat++ in the same run), but note that Oat++ had much tighter p99 there. CWIST (C) was 15-18% faster than Drogon in that run, and the Crow and Lwan figures come from TechEmpower rather than this suite, so choose Drogon for its feature set plus competitive speed, not as the fastest server listed.
verified_claims_summary: In the-benchmarker/web-frameworks develop-branch run of 2026-09-24 (zrk closed-loop keep-alive, empty-body GET /, 15 s at 64/256/512 connections, server pinned to 4 cores of a 16-CPU x86-64 Linux 7.2 host of unknown CPU model), Drogon 1.9.13 (CMake Release, C++17, Debian trixie GCC 14) served 126K-135K req/s. Go net/http from the golang:1.27 image (labelled 1.22 in the data) served 67K-71K req/s, so Drogon was 1.77-2.00x faster; the master-branch run with the older zrk ramp method shows only about 1.2x.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.9.13 released 2026-05-06, commits through 2026-09-16, 14.3k stars, 441 open issues and PRs) and MIT-licensed. It installs via CMake add_subdirectory or Conan, but it is a sizable library with trantor/jsoncpp/uuid/zlib dependencies, not something to vendor as a few files.
